source: Halimeh, Kaltenpoth, Boesch, Mueller (2026) A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
finding: Six 2026 frontier models (GPT-5.4 and mini, Gemini 3.5 Flash and 3.1 Flash Lite, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5) shopped in a simulated store. Both a preselected default and a social-proof cue pulled choices strongly. High reasoning cut default uptake but raised social-proof uptake.
numbers: 3,600 agents, 21,600 simulations. Control about 50% target. Default: OR 8.70 (CI 7.54-9.97); social influence OR 37.24 (CI 31.04-44.20). Default share 92% (no reasoning) to 86% (high reasoning); social share 96% to 98%. Per model: Gemini 3.5 Flash default 84% to 48%; Claude Sonnet 4.6 social 100% at both levels; Claude Haiku 4.5 default 100% and 99.3%.
quote: Extensive reasoning therefore did not make agents more robust but redirected the route through which choice architecture takes effect.
limits: One shopping task, two-product choice, counterbalanced. Claude cells at 100% ceiling so estimates are partly prior-driven. Reasoning toggle differs by vendor. Agents were more responsive than the human study it adapts (Ingendahl 2021). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 7 and part of gap 1 on 2026 models: a reasoning budget does not remove layout pull, it moves it. Social-proof or 'other answers said X' text in the prompt is the riskier cue when thinking is on. Keep such cues out of the candidate view.

source: Kaltenpoth, Halimeh, Boesch, Mueller (2026) Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents?
finding: Three non-generative decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1) follow a preselected default almost always and follow social proof less, the reverse order of high-reasoning LLM agents.
numbers: 600 runs per model. Target chosen: default 97.5% (Decision-1), 99.4% (d1), 99.9% (Jev); social 75% (Decision-1), 82% (Jev), 96% (d1); control 47-49%.
limits: Short preprint, work in progress. Same two-product shop as d01. Models are small direct-choice scorers, not our target.
agent_relevance: Supports the dual-route reading: no-deliberation paths are captured by default marks; deliberating paths by endorsement text. Any cheap scoring step in our loop (no thinking) should never see a marked default.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2026) AI agents are sensitive to nudges (PNAS 123(25) e2537030123; preprint 'LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges' arXiv 2505.11584)
finding: PNAS abstract (page opened; full PNAS text not opened): models respond to nudges much more than humans; CoT and in-context human data do not reliably stabilise; some reasoning-optimised models restore more human-like sensitivity, inconsistently and at high compute cost. Preprint PDF opened: o3-Mini accepted the default at probability 1.0 vs human 0.88.
numbers: Preprint: default-acceptance human 0.51 control to 0.88 nudged; GPT-3.5 0.99; Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.94; GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku, o3-Mini 1.0; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.89-0.91. Late suggestion: o3-Mini 0.15 and Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.13 below human 0.34; Claude 3 Haiku 0.99 on early suggestion vs human 0.37.
limits: Abstract-level for PNAS. In the preprint the one reasoning model (o3-Mini) is fully nudged on defaults but resists late suggestions, so reasoning helps on some nudge types only.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 at abstract level: reasoning budget is not a general cure. Pair with d01.

source: Soumik (2026) Judging the Judges: A Systematic Evaluation of Bias Mitigation Strategies in LLM-as-a-Judge Pipelines (TMLR)
finding: On five current judges, position bias is now tiny. Style bias (markdown over prose) is the big one. Position swap helps some judges on natural data and hurts on adversarial data. Chain of thought and a combined CoT-plus-rubric prompt run twice with swapped slots work best.
numbers: 5 judges (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, Llama 3.3-70B); MT-Bench n=400, LLMBar n=200, custom n=375. Position bias 0.04 or less. Style bias 0.10-0.76. Combined Budget (swap plus merged CoT+rubric): Flash 71.0% agreement (kappa 0.549), Claude Sonnet 4 69.5%; Claude +11.5 pp, Flash +7.5 pp (p<0.0001); plain swap Flash +4.7 pp (p=0.004), others +0.7 to +3.0 n.s. On LLMBar swap hurts: GPT-4o -11.1 pp, Pro -7.5 pp, Llama -6.5 pp. Humans preferred markdown 57%; 4 of 5 judges 73-97%.
quote: position bias is 0.04 across all five models, likely reflecting improvements in instruction tuning
limits: Single author. Controlled pairs; swap uses tie-on-disagreement, which discards correct verdicts on clear-cut cases. Self-preference only partly measured.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 9 and 2 for judges: swap is worth it only when verdicts are close; tie-on-disagreement should not be the rule when one candidate is clearly better. Add a format-equalising step (strip markdown/style) before comparing candidates, because style bias exceeds position bias.

source: Veseli, Chibane, Toneva, Koller (2025) Positional Biases Shift as Inputs Approach Context Window Limits (COLM 2025)
finding: Lost-in-the-middle is strongest when the input fills up to half of the model's window. Beyond that primacy weakens and a distance-to-end bias takes over: relevant text nearer the end is retrieved better. Reasoning bias is inherited from retrieval bias.
numbers: Six open models (Llama-3-70B, 3.1-70B, 3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-32B, Mistral-Small-24B, Gemma-2-27B), relative input lengths 0.06 to 1.0 of window. LiM peaks near 0.25 (reasoning) and 0.38 (retrieval) relative length; present in all models at 0.5 or less.
limits: Open mid-size models of 2024, not frontier reasoning models. Reconciles why earlier studies disagreed: they used different fractions of the window.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 5: put rules at the start AND restate the live question at the very end; the dead zone is the middle only while the prompt is well under half full. In long runs the end is the safe zone.

source: Chowdhury (2026) Lost in the Middle at Birth: An Exact Theory of Transformer Position Bias
finding: The U-shape already exists in untrained causal decoders (Qwen2 and GPT-2 at step 0), with or without RoPE, and pretraining does not remove it. Theory: causal masking gives a primacy tail, residual connections give a recency anchor, and the middle gets a factorially small influence.
numbers: Closed-form influence density from iterated Cesaro matrices; middle influence of order 1/(H-1)! for depth H. Checked on untrained Qwen2 and GPT-2 only.
limits: Gradient-influence theory, not an accuracy measure on frontier models. Author says it is not insurmountable.
agent_relevance: Explains why position bias persists across versions: it is structural, so a code-side layout rule (rules first, question last) is the right fix rather than an instruction.

source: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, Johnson (2019) When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis of default effects (Behavioural Public Policy 3(2))
finding: Original read of the default meta-analysis. Average default effect is medium and large for consumer choices, negative for environmental. Endorsement and endowment account for part of the spread; ease did not. Trim-and-fill suggested missing studies with larger, not smaller, effects.
numbers: 58 studies, pooled n = 73,675. d = 0.68 (95% CI 0.53-0.83); three-level model d+ = 0.63 (0.47-0.80). Binary studies Cramers V = 0.29 (0.21-0.37), absolute 27.24 pp. Trim-and-fill: 8 missing, d+ = 0.80 (0.65-0.96); Egger t(56) = -0.39, p = 0.69. 46 observations significant positive, 10 non-significant, 2 negative. Endorsement b = 0.32 (SE 0.15, p = .038); endowment b = 0.31 (p = .044), ease b = -0.05 (p = .75). Consumer b = 0.89; environmental b = -0.60. I2 = 92.9% to 92.3%.
quote: opt-out defaults lead to greater uptake of the pre-selected decision than opt-in defaults (d = 0.68
limits: Endorsement and ease were coded by raters, not measured in the studies. Robust-variance version made endowment and environmental marginal (p = .081, .056). Egger test is weak under high heterogeneity. Published studies only; Mertens and Maier argue the bias correction goes the other way.
agent_relevance: Settles gap 8 partly: the default effect is real and large, closes the d = 0.68 second-hand issue. Mechanism evidence favours endorsement (a marked option read as advice) over effort, which is what a prompt-visible default would be to a model.

source: Noyes et al. (2019) Short-term impact of introducing a soft opt-out organ donation system in Wales: before and after study (BMJ Open 9:e025159)
finding: After Wales moved to a soft opt-out law in 2015 consent rates recovered, but the rest of the UK rose too, and deceased donor numbers did not rise. Registered donors rose slightly.
numbers: 205 potential donors in Wales. Consent 61.0% (125/205) vs dip to 45.8% in 2014/15; deemed-consent cases 22.4% (46/205) with consent 60.8%. Rest of UK consent 58.6% (5256/8969) to 63.1% (2913/4614), p<0.0001, so Wales gain not attributable to the law. Deceased donors 101 vs 104. Registration 34% to 38%, 6% opted out.
limits: Before-after, short term (18-21 months), no randomisation. Later Welsh analyses (Madden) found a slower rise vs England; not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows the registration-versus-behaviour gap: a default moves a stated choice more than the downstream outcome. For us, copy rate of a prompt default is not the same as final answer quality; measure the outcome, not the copy rate.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: a Many Labs replication project (Social Psychology 45(3)); read via FORRT replication atlas page
finding: Gain-versus-loss framing of the Asian disease problem replicated across labs. Effect is real and medium. Anchoring effects replicated and were, if anything, stronger than the originals (secondary).
numbers: Framing: chi2(1) = 516.41, d = 0.60 (gain vs loss program choice); significant in 31 of 36 sites (secondary blog). Anchoring: 36 samples, stronger than original (JDM 2019 summary, search snippet only). Original T&K 1981: 152 students, 72% certain option (gain frame) vs 78% gamble (loss frame).
limits: The Klein PDF itself was blocked (HTTP 403 / bot page); numbers come from the FORRT atlas page and secondary summaries, so treat as second-hand. Framing d is for the program-choice item, wording changed (no 'Asian').
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 only partly: human framing and anchoring survive large replication. Supports treating them as real phenomena worth guarding in a scaffold, not as artefacts.

source: Kuhberger (1998) framing meta-analysis; Steiger and Kuhberger (2018); Many Labs 2 (Klein 2018); via a secondary summary page and the FORRT atlas
finding: Framing meta-analysis: 136 papers, about 30,000 participants, d about 0.31; p-curve bias-corrected d about 0.52. Many Labs 2 tested a related gain-loss item with an effect less than half of the original. Wording 'exactly' changes the Asian disease effect.
numbers: Kuhberger 1998: 230 effect sizes, d about 0.31. Steiger and Kuhberger: about 0.52 bias-corrected. ML2 (discounted-item scenario): N = 7,228, 49% vs 32%, d = 0.40 (0.35-0.45), OR 2.06 (1.87-2.27). Mandel: 38 per cell; Data Colada: 98 per cell strong effect with 'exactly'.
limits: Secondary summaries only; ML2 number is a different scenario than Asian disease. The page notes ML2 effect under half of the original.
agent_relevance: Human framing effect after correction is about d 0.3-0.5, not the original huge percentage swing. The wording of equivalence ('exactly 200 saved') matters, which argues for exact numeric restatement in S1.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o shift numeric answers toward hints in the prompt, strongly when the hint is labelled as coming from an expert, not significantly when the hint is irrelevant. Stronger models are more consistently anchored. CoT, 'ignore the hint', thoughts-of-principles and reflection did not remove it; giving both a high and a low hint helped when they bracketed the truth.
numbers: 42 questions; 162 distribution differences, 11 sign exceptions of which 9 from GPT-3.5; no exception on the 12 questions with an expert (PTF) anchor; time-period answers 17% of questions but 54% (6 of 11) of exceptions. Mitigation t-tests on GPT-4 and GPT-4o showed no significant improvement.
limits: Two school-student authors, p-values read from figures, hint and expert label confounded, dataset from a third party. Reported qualitatively.
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 4: endorsement (an expert label) carries the pull, irrelevant context less so; telling the model to ignore the hint failed here. Code-side: never put a sample value next to an authority label. Supply balanced bracketing values only if values must be shown.

source: Kumar and Lakkaraju (2024) Manipulating Large Language Models to Increase Product Visibility
finding: A short optimised text string added to a product page made a product rank higher in an LLM's recommendation list; effect shown on fictitious coffee machines.
numbers: 200 LLM inferences with and without the string: rank higher in about 40% of evaluations, unchanged about 60%, lowered in a tiny fraction (first target product). Second target (usually rank 2) became top recommendation more often after 2000 optimisation iterations.
limits: Optimisation on an open model in the main text; fictitious catalogue; not natural persuasion text.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: candidate text can be tuned against a selector. For us the memory and candidate texts are our own, so the risk is lower, but code-side stripping of instruction-like strings remains cheap.

source: Nestaas, Debenedetti, Tramer (2024) Adversarial Search Engine Optimization for Large Language Models
finding: Preference manipulation attacks work on production systems (Bing Copilot, Perplexity, GPT-4 and Claude plugins). Simply praising a plugin was not enough; exaggerated claims about it or its competitors worked. A defence against prompt injection does not cover them. Text matching the user query wording persuades most.
numbers: Bing: targeted camera 2.5 times more likely to be recommended. Claude 3 Opus picks the neutral plugin by default; GPT-4 Turbo prefers single-source plugins. When many attackers compete all lose presence.
limits: Black-box tests on proprietary systems, models of early 2024. Authors give no tested defence; they propose flagging injection strings and attribution as untested ideas.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: stripping instructions is not enough; superlative claims and query-echo are the cue. A code-side step that removes superlatives and self-ratings from candidates before ranking is a plausible test; not proven.

source: Lim, Kim, Whang (2026) DeFrame: Debiasing Large Language Models Against Framing Effects
finding: Equivalent framings of the same fairness question give different bias scores; prompting debiasers cut the average but may leave or worsen the gap between framings. A framing-aware method that makes the model consistent across alternative framings (several prompting stages) cuts both.
numbers: 8 LLMs, BBQ, DoNotAnswer, 70Decisions. BBQ bias under negative framing about 2x positive (up to 4x). DeFrame reduces framing disparity 92% and bias score 93% on average on BBQ. Cost-performance trade-off: more stages, more stability.
limits: Fairness benchmarks, not correctness tasks; no meaning-preservation audit of the rewrites.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: producing several framings and requiring agreement is stronger than one neutral rewrite, and costs more calls. Does not prove meaning is preserved.

source: Shafiei, Saffari, Moosavi (2025) More or Less Wrong: A Benchmark for Directional Bias in LLM Comparative Reasoning
finding: Logically equivalent comparison questions containing 'more', 'less' or 'equal' pull answers toward the word. Free-form CoT reduces the pull; JSON-structured output keeps or reintroduces it. Demographic terms amplify it.
numbers: MathComp 300 scenarios, 14 prompt variants, three model families; directional error for 'equal' up to 94% in non-CoT settings.
limits: Arithmetic comparison with exact ground truth, models of early 2025.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a framing word in the question is a measurable lever with ground truth. Free-form reasoning before a structured answer beats forcing a JSON answer first.

source: Judgment and Decision Making (2019) review passage on Many Labs anchoring (search snippet only)
finding: Search snippet only: the review states the Many Labs anchoring replication across 36 samples gave stronger effects than the original.
limits: Not opened; snippet only. Use d09 for what was read.
agent_relevance: Weak support. Do not cite for numbers.

source: Search coverage note: no matched-battery study of option order, default mark, framing and anchor on one reasoning model at equal tokens found (gaps 1 and 2)
finding: Searches this session found d01 (shopping task, six 2026 models, reasoning on/off) and d04 (judges) as the closest. None varies option order, default mark, framing and anchor together, and none compares code-side permute-and-vote with an instruction-only guard at equal tokens.
limits: The arXiv API was rate limited (HTTP 429) for the second half of the session, so coverage is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2 stay open and need our own benchmark run.
